In case anyone has questions! Possibly this should go in "Machine learning for theorem proving", as this was mainly a project so that I could get experience with recent Claude Code.

https://github.com/girving/aks

#announce > Seiferas's simplified O(log n) depth sorting networks @ 💬

Not yet, but it’s on my todo list! Do you have a favorite? I also plan to run it through an independent proof checker.
Is https://github.com/GasStationManager/SafeVerify the right thing to use? Cc @GasStationManager.
You can run it through both the learn kernel and nanoda with https://github.com/leanprover/comparator/.

Perfect, will try that today or tomorrow hopefully.

@Geoffrey Irving this would be a perfect fit for VibeRegistry, a public registry of AI-assisted Lean proofs that will verify with both SafeVerify and Comparator as part of its CI. To try it locally, you'd want to clone the repo, and put in an entry containing your spec files (those theorem statements with sorries that you'd create anyway for use with comparator or SafeVerify). Or if you have the spec, I'm happy to add it.

@Kevin Buzzard Do you know if Ramanujan graphs are still significantly out of reach for current Mathlib? My assumption is yes unless there are simpler modern constructions that my searches haven’t found yet.
Does #36335 help?
We don't have any spectral graph theory yet AFAIK, but we do have docs#SimpleGraph.Connected / docs#SimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree / docs#SimpleGraph.adjMatrix
The repo already contains basic spectral graph theory and two different expander families: zigzag and MGG. Just not the super hard stuff that needs deep number theory.

    net.size ≤ 705 * 10 ^ 61 * n * Nat.clog 2 n := sorry

Is there a standard recipe for running comparator as part of Github CI?
Not at the moment no, but I would be happy to accept a template as a PR
This looks very interesting.
I am not sure I would have done any of these things this way (having done a little work in the area) but it's still very cool that this could all be generated.
I'm certainly interested at a good formalisation of comparator networks and sorting networks at some point

I think the interfaces themselves are mostly clean. Formally Claude wrote all the lines of code for them as well, but I needed to make a bunch of super detailed suggestions. When I didn’t in some area of the codebase, it would produce a terrible definition and then get very bogged down trying to prove messier things.

Wrenna Robson said:

I am not sure I would have done any of these things this way (having done a little work in the area) but it's still very cool that this could all be generated.

What different routes would you have gone?
So, hmm. I'm not sure that Fin n -> A style tuples are the best models here. I think I prefer focusing on Vector, because it's much more natural to apply swaps in place there.

It’s pretty easy to change out the definitions: most of the actual proof uses either the 01-principle or sorting of permutations (AKS/Sort/ZeroOne.lean and AKS/Sort/Perm.lean show these are equivalent).
Yes. I like the result about sorting perms being enough.
https://github.com/bristolcrypto/controlbits/tree/main/verification/PermNetwork this is much smaller but might be of interest
https://github.com/bristolcrypto/controlbits/blob/main/verification/PermNetwork/PermNetwork/ComparatorNetwork/Basic.lean
Sorry here specifically
Despite what I just said this does use tuples but as you say that isn't too bad to fix

I don't know if you have an equivalent of permOn_cSwaps_map_of_monotone_cSwaps but I think it's worth having as it actually has practical use. It basically says that if you have a sorting network, and apply a permutation to its comparators, then the resulting comparator network "sorts up to that permutation"
Which is useful in practice for SIMD optimisation.

(because a well-chosen permutation lets you move your comparators into a SIMD-favourable configuration - this isn't quite my area, the student I worked with, Sam Kelly, he's got a much better head for the practical details here, but that's the gist)
I probably don’t have that, but I would have to check to be sure (Claude wrote a bunch of lemmas about how networks interact with subsets of wires and such as part of the bag tree work).
I'm also not entirely sure if comparator should have i < j. That's the basic definition. But in the bitonic network normally you have comparators in both directions.
It might be better to just define it as an index pair and then deal accordingly with direction as a property of it

I did go back and forth on this though - my gut is that ultimately it's nicer to have the type of a comparator to be as simple as possible. Actually arguably it would be even nicer to not use Fin n but Nat, because in theory a comparator of a larger size than your tuple/vector is fine, it just doesn't do anything. And it would mean you'd have zero issues with typecast juggling.
Still it does look like Claude has done an admirable job, it's very cool that this is possible.

One thing I have been inching towards for some time but I haven't yet found a way of stating it I am certain I like is how to say "X is the sorted version of Y" without providing a concrete sorting function. It would be nice to unify how we treat sorts including sorting networks.

Yep. Also it would be better to have an exec definition that worked on non-total orders in the expected way: the min/max definition does not do the right thing in all cases.

I wouldn’t attribute too much to Claude on the definition quality front: some of it is Claude, but a lot of it required correction.
That makes sense. I do think API and overall design is harder for them than nodding-dog "fill out the theorems" work (but they're very good at that!)

My current position on AI with formal methods (in either direction) I think, having been thinking about this a lot lately, is that it's clearly got a lot of potential but you need brain very firmly turned on, and I am a little concerned not everyone is doing that.
The biggest piece that was close to autonomous was MGG, though I still had to handhold it to get it to not build definitions and proofs that didn’t massively time out.

Geoffrey Irving said:

Yep. Also it would be better to have an exec definition that worked on non-total orders in the expected way: the min/max definition does not do the right thing in all cases.

I wouldn’t attribute too much to Claude on the definition quality front: some of it is Claude, but a lot of it required correction.

Yes, working out exactly what you want to require from your order is tough. Clearly total orders are very nice but intuitively you can still at least try to perform a sort even if it isn't total
All you have to do is branch once and then preserve the identity of objects flowing along the wires, so that two things that compare equally all survive.

A theorem I would really like is something like the following: if you have a permutation pi, and sort the tuples (pi i, i), then the ith element in the resulting list is (i, pi^-1 i). Which is basically why sorts are enough to invert a permutation in a pinch - constant time with sorting networks!
It's easy to see why this is true but I've found it quite annoying to actually state and prove. Maybe I just need to sit down and Just Do It or even ask an AI to find a short route to begin with.
Certainly Claude Opus 4.6 is strong enough to prove that kind of thing. E.g., AKS/Sort/Perm.lean was generated autonomously based on a few-sentence natural language request.
I've found it a little mixed. Sometimes there's something that I proved pretty easily they get stuck on and sometimes they succeed easily at something I'm tangled in.

Notably that Perm success was well into the project, after a ton of iteration on CLAUDE.md and such. And yes, that level lemma don’t always work.

In that particular case Claude was flailing trying to prove some bag tree stuff and I managed to get it to explain that one of the obstacles was dealing with sorting of non-permutations, so it also had some surrounding proof context to help with intuition.
Watching the other threads with various holes poked in semi-automated proofs, I have to say I’m relieved that no one’s falsified my AKS one yet…
When I'm back from Taiwan I can give it a closer look if you like
I've had no brain for Big Thoughts this week

@Henrik Böving I added a Github workflow to the repo that runs comparator:

  1. Currently passes: https://github.com/girving/aks
  2. Workflow: https://github.com/girving/aks/blob/main/.github/workflows/comparator.yml
  3. A patch I needed to make to comparator to get it running on Github workers: https://github.com/girving/comparator/commit/15e20b1d86bad1c72f538dbb16791d00fada4d66

I'm not sure if the patch is appropriate: it might be weakening the sandbox a bit. I do think the sequencing is right in terms of downloading Mathlib first but otherwise only building AKS within the sandbox.
It does open up the possibility of e.g. spawning a gdb (or other debugger of your choosing) and using it to infiltrate the checking process yes.
Without it, I get permission errors inside landrun when comparator tries to run processes (not at the computer so I don’t have the specifics). So some patch is required unfortunately.
Do you understand why the add-exec doesn't work? It's not like the procedure is magic
If it’s not magic, I would advise disabling —best-effort. :)

The --add-exec not working was because when I switched from my local machine where it worked to Github, I also accidentally switched to the last released version of landrun. They've fixed bugs in --add-exec in master that are not released, specifically handling of exec permissions for dynamic libraries. Now I'm building landrun from source and it works fine with HEAD comparator within Github actions:

https://github.com/girving/aks/commit/99560253b8c0f55074b16574bb7720960915643d

I have not investigated whether --best-effort is required as yet.
